paras: The whitecapping of William Noblett was a whitecap raid near Farmington, Marshall County, Tennessee, in the autumn of 1903, in which a band of men badly beat Noblett, a Black man, and his wife. Seven men from neighboring Bedford County were arrested, and in November 1903 a Marshall County grand jury indicted them while the governor appointed a special assistant to the prosecution. A December 1904 report that five men with matching names had been sentenced to four months in jail for whitecapping indicates that the case ended in convictions.

Farmington lay near the line between Marshall and Bedford counties, and a Lewisburg dispatch to the Columbia Herald said all of the accused lived in the Eighteenth district of Bedford County. The only cause given in the coverage came from the Bolivar Bulletin, which said the men had whitecapped Noblett "about a dog" without explaining further.

The raid is not dated in the surviving reports, but it took place before a preliminary hearing held in the week before October 30 and "several weeks" before November 18, 1903. According to the Columbia Herald, the county was "stirred up" over the raid, in which "a negro, William Noblett, and his wife were badly beaten." The coverage does not describe the couple's injuries or say how many men took part in the raid itself.

Seven men were arrested shortly afterward and given a preliminary hearing before a magistrate at Farmington. On November 18, 1903, the grand jury at Lewisburg returned indictments against all of the suspects, and a hearing was set for that Friday. Governor Frazier appointed C. A. Armstrong to assist Attorney General Falkner in the prosecution.

No report of the trial itself was found. In December 1904 the Columbia Herald reported that Jim Glasscock, Bob and Rose Darnell, and George and Will Chives had each been sentenced to four months in jail at Lewisburg for whitecapping. That brief did not name the victims, but all five names appear among the men charged in the Farmington case.

The case was reported only in white Tennessee papers, and no Black-press coverage was found. The Columbia Herald gave it the fullest treatment under the headline "WILL PUNISH WHITE CAPPERS," with a subhead on men "Suspected of Beating Up Farmington Negroes," and called the raid "the outrage." The Bolivar Bulletin ran two short court notes, "Whitecappers Bound Over" in October and "Half Dozen Indicted" in November, the second describing the victims only as "a negro and his wife." None of the reports gave the couple's own account of the attack, and the 1904 sentencing note did not mention them at all.

The papers differ on the result of the preliminary hearing: the Bolivar Bulletin, writing within about a week of it, said the men were bound over to Circuit Court in bonds of $1,000 each, while the Columbia Herald said they were released. The lists of the accused also vary, with the October report naming Jim Glasscock where the Herald named Claud Cheves, and the November Bulletin brief listing only six men.
